sources.title: Parker Pearson et al. (2024), Stonehenge and its Altar Stone: the significance of distant stone sources, Archaeology International
Ancient Britons May Have Built Stonehenge to Symbolize Unity

facts.text: Building at Stonehenge began about 5,000 years ago, and the monument was changed and added to over roughly the next 2,000 years.
Some archaeologists have thought Stonehenge was a temple, an observatory or a solar calendar. It was also the largest burial ground in Britain of its time.
The first stones put up at Stonehenge, around 3000 BCE, were bluestones from the Preseli Hills in west Wales. There are 43 bluestones, and their source is about 225 km away.
The huge sarsen stones came from about 24 km to the north of the monument.
The Altar Stone weighs about six tonnes, and for about a century it was believed to have come from Wales.

In 2024, scientists dated and analysed tiny mineral grains from pieces of the Altar Stone. The grains’ ages and chemistry matched sandstone from the Orcadian Basin, a region of northeast Scotland, and did not match rocks from Wales.
The Altar Stone travelled at least 700 km; no other stone in a monument of that age is known to have been moved so far. Its exact source in Scotland and how it was moved are still unknown.
The wheel had not yet reached Britain, so moving the stones would have needed hundreds or even thousands of people.
In December 2024, Mike Parker Pearson and colleagues argued in the journal Archaeology International that Stonehenge may have served politics as well as religion, by uniting the peoples of Britain.
Among more than 900 stone circles in Britain, Stonehenge is the only one whose stones all came from distant regions.
The Altar Stone lies flat, like the large horizontal stones of the recumbent stone circles, a type found only in northeast Scotland.
The researchers suggest the Altar Stone may have been a gift from Neolithic people in northern Scotland, perhaps to strengthen an alliance.
People from many parts of Britain brought pigs and cattle to winter feasts at Durrington Walls, a large Neolithic village near Stonehenge.
Close to half of those whose remains lie at Stonehenge had spent part of their lives away from Salisbury Plain.

The second main building stage, around 2500 BCE, came at a time when newcomers from what are now the Netherlands and Germany arrived, bringing metalworking. The researchers suggest the monument may have been a response meant to unite the native Britons.
The authors note that such unification could have been reached by force or by consent, and they think a gift is the more likely explanation for the Altar Stone.
